items.m03s3q4: Overall, the Science Museum enjoyed sustained growth in visitor numbers across the decade, in marked contrast to the Art Gallery and the History Museum, both of which declined gradually. Having begun as the second most popular venue, the Science Museum overtook the Art Gallery around the midpoint of the period, while the History Museum remained the least visited throughout.
items.m03s3q5: Overall, the country's electricity mix shifted markedly away from coal, whose share fell by more than half, towards natural gas and renewables. Natural gas emerged as the leading source by the end of the period, and wind and solar rose from a negligible contribution to one of the largest, whereas nuclear and hydro remained virtually unchanged.
items.m03ckq8: Overall, the youngest group devoted the most time to social media and gaming, and both of these activities declined steeply with age. Streaming video, by contrast, was strikingly consistent across the four age groups, which made it the dominant activity among those aged 30 and over.
items.m04s3q5: Visitor numbers at the Science Museum rose from just over 400 thousand in 2010 to approximately 760 thousand a decade later, nearly doubling over the period.
items.m04s3q6: People aged 13 to 17 spent 21 hours a week on social media, more than three times as long as the 6 hours recorded for those aged 50 and over.
items.m04ckq8: Coal's share of electricity generation fell from 48% in 2000 to 18% in 2020, a decline of 30 percentage points over the two decades.
items.m06s3q7: In 2010 the Science Museum attracted approximately 420 thousand visitors, considerably fewer than the Art Gallery's 610 thousand. Its attendance then rose steadily, overtaking the Art Gallery in 2014 at 570 thousand compared with 560 thousand, and continued upwards to a peak of 760 thousand in 2020, almost twice its initial figure. By the end of the period it drew nearly three times as many visitors as the History Museum, which had fallen to 260 thousand.
items.m07s3q7: German teachers were the best remunerated at both stages, with salaries of 62000 and 81000 dollars at the start and after 15 years respectively. Thai teachers, by contrast, earned by far the least, at 9000 and 17000 dollars, meaning that a newly qualified German teacher was paid roughly seven times as much as a Thai counterpart. Japan, Korea and the USA occupied the middle ground, with starting salaries of 31000, 33000 and 44000 dollars.
items.m08s3q7: Overall, the recycling of glass bottles is a cyclical, man-made process comprising eight stages, which fall into two broad phases: preparing the waste glass and manufacturing the new product. The cycle begins with the collection of used bottles at a bottle bank and ends when the new bottles are filled and delivered to shops, whereupon it repeats.
items.m09s3q7: Overall, the centre of Riverside underwent a transformation from an industrial and commercial district into a predominantly residential and leisure area. The factory was replaced by apartment blocks, and traffic was removed from the centre through the pedestrianisation of the main road and the construction of a ring road, whereas the river, the park and the bus station remained where they were.
items.m10s3q7: Finland consumed by far the most coffee, at 21 cups per person per week, half as much again as Italy, which ranked second with 14 cups. Brazil was close behind on 12 cups, whereas Japan and Thailand lagged well behind at 8 and 5 cups respectively. Thai consumption was therefore less than a quarter of the Finnish figure and barely a third of the Italian one.

plan.big: Science Museum rose steadily throughout; Art Gallery and History Museum both declined; crossover around 2014

slots.what: how many people, in thousands, visited three museums in a European city
slots.groupB: the Art Gallery and the History Museum
slots.feature: the Science Museum overtook the Art Gallery around 2014 and finished the period as the most visited of the three

p-line-museums.text:
The line graph illustrates how many people, in thousands, visited three museums in a European city over the ten-year period from 2010 to 2020.

Overall, the Science Museum attracted steadily more visitors throughout the decade, whereas both the Art Gallery and the History Museum declined. The Science Museum overtook the Art Gallery around 2014 and finished the period as the most popular of the three, while the History Museum remained the least visited.

In 2010, the Science Museum received 420 thousand visitors, the lowest figure apart from the History Museum. Its numbers then rose every two years, reaching 570 thousand in 2014 and 710 thousand in 2018, before peaking at 760 thousand in 2020, which was almost double the starting figure.

By contrast, the Art Gallery, which had been the most visited museum in 2010 with 610 thousand visitors, fell gradually to 520 thousand by 2020, despite a slight recovery in 2016. The History Museum followed a similar downward path, dropping from 380 thousand to 260 thousand over the same period, with a brief rise to 300 thousand in 2018.

By contrast, the Art Gallery, which had been the most visited in 2010 with 610 thousand visitors, fell gradually to 520 thousand by 2020, while the History Museum, the least visited throughout, dropped from 380 thousand to 260 thousand over the same period, with a brief rise to 300 thousand in 2018.

plan.big: social media and gaming fall steeply with age; streaming is flat across groups and leads for the over-30s

slots.what: the average weekly hours that four age groups in one country devoted to social media, streaming video and gaming in 2023
slots.contrast: time on social media and gaming fell steeply with age, whereas streaming varied little between the groups
slots.figA: 21 hours for teenagers, compared with 6 hours for the over-50s
slots.figB: between 12 and 15 hours in every group
slots.exception: streaming video, which was the leading activity for everyone aged 30 and over

p-bar-screentime.text:
The bar chart compares the average weekly hours that four age groups in one country devoted to social media, streaming video and gaming in 2023.

Overall, time spent on social media and gaming fell steeply with age, with teenagers the heaviest users of both. Streaming video, by contrast, varied little between the groups and was the leading activity for everyone aged 30 and over.

Social media was the most popular activity among the young, at 21 hours a week for 13–17-year-olds and 18 hours for the 18–29 group, but this fell to 11 hours for those aged 30–49 and only 6 hours for the over-50s. Gaming declined even more sharply, from 12 hours for teenagers to just 1 hour for the oldest group.

Streaming video, which ranged from 12 to 15 hours in every group, was the exception. The 18–29 group watched the most, at 15 hours, while the 30–49 group watched the least, at 12 hours; for those aged 50 and over, streaming, at 13 hours, took almost twice as long as social media and gaming combined.

plan.big: man-made cyclical process, eight stages, from bottle bank to delivery; two phases, preparing waste glass and making new bottles

slots.product: how used glass bottles are recycled into new ones
slots.start: the collection of empty bottles at a bottle bank
slots.st1: used bottles are deposited in a bottle bank and transported by lorry to a recycling plant
slots.st2: they are washed with high-pressure water
slots.st3: they are sorted by colour into clear, green and brown glass and crushed into small pieces known as cullet
slots.st4: is melted in a furnace at 600–800 °C together with new raw materials
slots.st5: the molten glass is moulded into new bottles
slots.st6: the bottles are filled and delivered to shops, after which the cycle begins again

p-proc-glass.text:
The diagram illustrates the stages by which used glass bottles are collected and turned into new ones.

Overall, this is a man-made, cyclical process with eight stages, beginning with the collection of empty bottles at a bottle bank and ending with new bottles being delivered to shops. The stages fall into two phases: the first four prepare the waste glass, while the last four create the new product.

At the first stage, used bottles are deposited in a bottle bank, from where they are transported by lorry to a recycling plant. Once there, the bottles are washed with high-pressure water and then sorted by colour into clear, green and brown glass. The sorted glass is then crushed into small pieces known as cullet.

In the second phase, the cullet is melted in a furnace at 600–800 °C, and new raw materials are added at this point. The molten glass is then moulded into new bottles, which are filled and delivered to shops, after which the cycle begins again when the empty bottles are returned to the bottle bank.

The molten glass is then moulded into new bottles, which are filled and delivered to shops, after which the cycle begins again when the empty bottles are returned to the bottle bank.

plan.big: the centre became far more modern and built-up; old buildings replaced on the same sites; river and temple unchanged; transport upgraded
plan.ga: north of the road: market, open field, temple, main road
plan.gb: south of the road: wooden houses, rice fields, ferry

slots.place: the centre of a small town in the north-east of Thailand
slots.change: became far more modern and built-up, with most old buildings replaced on the same sites
slots.where2: south-east, on the western part of the rice fields
slots.extended: the main road, which runs east from the river, was widened to four lanes
slots.converted: the open field beside the market

p-map-thai-town.text:
The two maps compare the centre of a small Thai town in the north-east of the country in 2005 and in 2025.

Overall, the town centre became far more modern and built-up, with most old buildings replaced on the same sites and a hospital occupying much of the former farmland. The river and the temple, however, remained unchanged, while transport links were upgraded.

To the north of the main road, the wet market in the west was rebuilt as a covered market, and the open field beside it was converted into a car park. The temple in the north-east corner stayed exactly where it was. The road itself, which runs from the river eastwards through the whole centre, was widened to four lanes.

South of the road, the wooden houses in the south-west were demolished and replaced by townhouses, and a new hospital was built on the western part of the rice fields in the south-east, which shrank to a narrow strip in the corner. Finally, the ferry crossing on the river was replaced by a road bridge in the same position.

plan.big: smartphones rose dramatically while basic phones fell by a similar amount; lines crossed between 2013 and 2016; near-mirror images

slots.what: what percentage of teenagers in one country owned a smartphone and what percentage owned a basic mobile phone
slots.feature: the two lines crossed between 2013 and 2016, and by 2025 nearly every teenager had a smartphone

p-line-phones.text:
The line graph shows what percentage of teenagers in one country owned a smartphone, and what percentage owned a basic mobile phone, over the fifteen years from 2010 to 2025.

Overall, smartphone ownership rose dramatically over the period while basic phone ownership fell by a similar amount, so that the two trends were almost mirror images of each other. The lines crossed between 2013 and 2016, and by 2025 nearly every teenager had a smartphone and very few still used a basic phone.

In 2010, only 10% of teenagers owned a smartphone. This figure tripled to 30% by 2013 and doubled again to 60% in 2016, which was the first year in which smartphones were more common than basic phones. Growth then slowed, with ownership reaching 80% in 2019, 90% in 2022 and finally 95% in 2025.

Basic phones followed the opposite path. Having stood at 80% in 2010, ownership dropped to 65% in 2013 and to 40% in 2016, before falling to 20% in 2019 and just 10% in 2022; by 2025 only 5% of teenagers owned one.

mocks.mock1:
The line graph shows the proportion of households with an internet connection in four countries, Sweden, Japan, Thailand and Kenya, over the twenty years from 2005 to 2025.

Overall, internet access rose in all four countries over the period. Sweden and Japan were already high at the start and converged at almost universal access by 2025, whereas Thailand recorded the most dramatic growth and Kenya, despite rising strongly, remained the lowest throughout.

Sweden had the highest figure in every year, climbing from 70% of households in 2005 to 85% in 2010 and 97% in 2025. Japan started lower, at 60%, but grew faster in the first five years, reaching 78% in 2010; by 2025 it stood at 95%, only two percentage points behind Sweden.

In contrast, only 12% of Thai households were online in 2005. Access then roughly doubled every five years to 52% in 2015 and climbed to 88% by 2025, which was close to the Japanese figure. Kenya began at just 2% and, although it rose to 35% in 2020 and 52% in 2025, ended the period where Thailand had been a decade earlier.
mocks.mock2:
The table gives information about the quantity of rice, in millions of tonnes, produced by China, India, Vietnam and Thailand in 2000, 2010 and 2020.

Overall, China was by far the largest producer in every year, although India recorded the biggest increase over the two decades. Vietnam and Thailand produced only a fraction of the two giants' output, and Thailand was the only country whose production declined between 2010 and 2020.

China's output rose steadily from 188 million tonnes in 2000 to 197 million in 2010 and 212 million in 2020. India, which began the period at 127 million tonnes, grew more quickly, reaching 144 million in 2010 and 178 million in 2020, an overall rise of more than 50 million tonnes.

The two smaller producers were on a different scale. Vietnam's output increased modestly, from 32 million tonnes to 40 million in 2010 and 43 million in 2020, whereas Thailand's rose from 26 million to 36 million in 2010 before falling back to 30 million in 2020, leaving it the smallest producer of the four.
mocks.mock3:
The two maps show the current layout of a secondary school campus and the changes that are planned for the site.

Overall, the plan adds buildings and green space at the expense of the sports field, which will lose half its area. The library and the car park will both be relocated, while the main building and the road along the western edge will remain as they are.

At present, the main building stands in the north-west corner beside the road, with the car park to its east. In the centre, the library and the canteen sit side by side, with open ground to the east of them, and the sports field stretches across the whole southern part of the site.

Under the plan, the car park will be converted into a garden, and a new car park will be built on the open ground in the centre-east. The canteen will be extended westwards into the space now occupied by the library, which will move to a larger new building in the south-west, so the sports field will be reduced to the south-eastern half of its current site.
